title: When the Winter Falls
premise: Freya Sandoval, a property surveyor raised by her grandmother after her parents vanished, is hired to appraise the family's ancestral house in the frost-bound town of Hollowmere — a house whose rooms rearrange and whose photographs keep gaining an extra chair. She discovers the founders bound something beneath the house with a ritual left deliberately unfinished, and that every Sandoval has been slowly erased from memory and record to feed it. When her grandmother's mind finally gives out and Freya's own name begins fading from documents and minds alike, she must choose between completing the ritual as a sacrifice or breaking it entirely. In the end she finishes it differently than intended — binding the thing not to a bloodline but to herself willingly, trading her old identity for a new one, and walking out of the house alive but unremembered by everyone except the one person who loved her enough to hold on.
about_author: Theo Eastwick is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing structural anomalies in New England houses before turning to horror full-time. Their work explores how architecture remembers what people try to forget.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Sorting her grandmother's photographs for the estate appraisal, Freya notices an unfamiliar wooden chair appearing in pictures spanning decades — always closer to the camera. She tells herself it's a duplicate print, a trick of light. Emotional beat: the quiet dread of a rational person watching their explanations run out.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Freya drives to the town to survey the house officially. The locals are polite but evasive; the town clerk can't find her grandmother's birth record. POV Freya. Beat: isolation tightening — she's surrounded by people who look through her.

chapters.title: Rooms That Count Differently
chapters.summary: Freya measures the house; the square footage never adds up twice the same way. She finds a sealed door behind lath and plaster, cold to the touch. POV Freya. Beat: professional competence curdling into fear as her instruments betray her.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept Saying
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Freya's POV, memories of childhood visits: grandmother counting chairs aloud each night, salting thresholds, whispering 'don't finish it.' Present-day Freya realizes the rituals were maintenance, not madness. Beat: grief reframed as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: In the attic, Freya finds a ledger kept by the house's builders, the Sandovals-by-marriage: entries describing a binding ritual begun in 1847 and pages torn out at the final step. POV Freya. Beat: hope — there are instructions — undercut by the missing ending.

chapters.title: Neighbor at the Fence
chapters.summary: POV shift to Idris Vane, an elderly neighbor who has watched the house for sixty years. He warns Freya that the chair belongs to 'the Tallyman,' who counts the household and takes what isn't claimed. Beat: first confirmation she isn't imagining it.

chapters.title: Her Name, Missing
chapters.summary: Freya's bank card declines; her employer has no record of hiring her; her phone contacts list her under 'unknown.' POV Freya. Beat: identity horror — the erasure has started, and it's eating her from the edges inward.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves
chapters.summary: Freya wakes to find the extra chair physically present in the kitchen, positioned facing her bed upstairs. Frost on its seat in the shape of a handprint. POV Freya. Beat: the haunting stops being archival and becomes intimate.

chapters.title: Idris's Confession
chapters.summary: Idris reveals he was engaged to Freya's great-aunt, who completed half the ritual in 1963 and was taken. He kept her notes hidden out of guilt. POV Idris. Beat: survivor's guilt and the cost of loving someone marked by the house.

chapters.title: Aunt Wren's Notes
chapters.summary: Freya deciphers Wren's notebook: the ritual requires a willing heir to speak the founders' words at the hearth on the winter solstice, then sit in the chair. Half-finished bindings fail and feed the thing instead. POV Freya. Beat: understanding the trap — finishing it may be exactly what it wants.

chapters.title: Frost Patterns
chapters.summary: Windows frost over in repeating geometric patterns that match the ledger's diagrams — a countdown. Each morning the pattern completes another ring. POV Freya. Beat: dread made visible; time is running out.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot Her
chapters.summary: Freya seeks help in Hollowmere; no one recognizes her, and the clerk now insists the house has stood empty for forty years. Only a child sees her and asks if she lives with 'the counting man.' POV Freya. Beat: total social erasure, loneliness sharpened into terror.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: Dream sequence bleeding into waking: Freya experiences the house's memory — the founders' bargain, a famine winter, something beneath the cellar offered survival in exchange for a counted soul each generation. POV Freya. Beat: sympathy for the monster's origin without forgiveness.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Last Night
chapters.summary: Freya visits her grandmother in care; the old woman surfaces from dementia long enough to say: 'Don't finish his sentence. Write your own.' Then she forgets Freya's face forever. POV Freya. Beat: heartbreak; the last anchor to her old self dissolving.

chapters.title: Idris Decides
chapters.summary: Idris offers to take Wren's place and sit in the chair himself, arguing he owes a debt sixty years overdue. Freya refuses to let him — and realizes refusal itself is a form of love the ritual doesn't account for. POV Idris. Beat: love against duty, stated plainly.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: The final frost ring closes. The house's interior rearranges around Freya, corridors folding toward the hearth whether she wills it or not. She prepares the ritual using both the ledger and Wren's corrections. POV Freya. Beat: grim resolve; she walks toward the trap with open eyes.

chapters.title: The Hearth
chapters.summary: Climax part one. At midnight Freya speaks the founders' words but alters them mid-sentence, per her grandmother's advice — claiming the house rather than offering herself. The Tallyman manifests as a figure of frost and furniture-wood, seated in the chair, and rises. POV Freya. Beat: defiance meeting consequence.

chapters.title: The Counting Man
chapters.summary: Climax part two. The Tallyman hunts her through the folding house, reciting names of every Sandoval taken. Freya reaches the cellar, finds the original bargain-seal, and understands: the thing isn't fed by sacrifice but by being remembered wrongly. POV Freya. Beat: terror transmuting into insight.

chapters.title: Writing Her Own Sentence
chapters.summary: Freya breaks the seal and rebinds the entity with new words — naming it truthfully, giving it a story instead of a hunger — then sits in the chair voluntarily, not as prey but as witness. The house goes still. POV Freya. Beat: courage as authorship; she survives by refusing the terms.

chapters.title: After the Thaw
chapters.summary: Morning. The house is ordinary, measurable, warm. The extra chair is gone from every photograph. Freya's records are restored — except her surname, which now reads only 'S.' POV Freya. Beat: exhausted relief shadowed by permanent change.

chapters.title: The One Who Held On
chapters.summary: POV Idris. He greets Freya at the fence by name — the only person in the world who still knows it. They share tea in the kitchen where the chair used to be. Beat: quiet, earned tenderness; love persisting past erasure.

chapters.title: When the Winter Falls
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Freya's POV, one year later. Freya stays in Hollowmere as its unofficial keeper, teaching the house her name nightly so it can't be unwritten again. First snow falls; the windows stay clear. Final beat: peace that must be maintained — inheritance transformed into choice.
